newsitem.title: USA: Selection of Oklahoma bombing jury completed.
newsitem.headline: Selection of Oklahoma bombing jury completed.

text.p: Ten men and eight women were picked on Tuesday to form the jury and alternates that will decide the murder and conspiracy case against Timothy McVeigh, accused of the Oklahoma City bombing that killed 168 people.

The panellists, whose identities have been kept secret through extraordinary measures, will be sworn in Thursday morning, when opening statements are expected in the trial before U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch.
Wednesday will be a day off for jurors to get their personal affairs in order, such as notifying their employers. Wednesday is also McVeigh's 29th birthday.
Referred to only by numbers, the jurors appeared behind a makeshift wall to conceal them from the media, which is confined to one side of the courtroom.

The gender breakdown could only be determined by their voices and non-media spectators on the far side of the crowded room. It also appeared that the group included one Hispanic and one Native American.
They will not be sequestered during the trial, which is expected to last four or five months.
As each juror entered the room, they were greeted with smiles by prosecutors, while McVeigh and his defence attorneys were expressionless.

The tall, pale McVeigh appeared, as he often has, to be actively involved in the proceedings. He frequently jotted down notes and wrote messages on bits of paper to the team of attorneys seated with him at the defence table.

The decorated Gulf War veteran is charged with setting the bomb that exploded at 9:02 a.m. on April 19, 1995, at the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City. Of the 168 dead, 19 were children, many of whom had just been dropped off at a day-care centre on the building's second floor.
McVeigh, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, faces the death penalty if convicted.

Outside the courtroom, the mother of a woman killed in the blast cried as she told reporters she is worried that a recent report citing failings at the FBI lab in Washington may weaken the government's case against the accused bomber.

"There are things that might not be used because somebody didn't do their job right, and it was my daughter's life," said Marsha Kight, whose daughter, Frankie Merrell, worked in a credit union in the federal building.

While prosecutors and defence attorneys are forbidden to talk about the case under a gag order imposed by the judge, the prosecution's case is believed to rely heavily on evidence allegedly linking McVeigh to the rental truck used in the bombing, to telephone calls made to find ingredients for the powerful bomb, and to the testimony of Michael Fortier, a friend who has said he knew McVeigh was planning the bombing.
Victims' family members Kight and Roy Sells, whose wife Lee died in the blast, also said outside the courtroom they were anxious about seeing graphic evidence likely to be introduced.
"They're going to be showing bad things, and I'm going to be remembering, so I know it's going to be tough," said Sells.

The painstaking selection process began months ago with the summoning of 1,000 potential jurors, about half of whom then filled out a 40-page questionnaire. Of those, 99 were interviewed by the judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys over the last three weeks.
In an effort to further protect their identities, the judge shuffled the jurors' numbers to obscure details revealed during the extensive questioning about their lives and backgrounds.

Potential jurors were given one last chance on Tuesday to be excused from serving, and one woman, who described herself as a caretaker, said she could not be impartial and was likely to side with the victims.
Another woman and two men, one a financial analyst and the other believed to be a window-washer, said serving on the trial would be financially disastrous.
